claim: Three Lunar Roving Vehicles (LRVs, 'lunar rovers') were driven on the Moon, one on each of Apollo 15 (David Scott and Jim Irwin, 1971), Apollo 16 (John Young and Charles Duke, 1972) and Apollo 17 (Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, 1972). NASA calls it a battery-powered vehicle. It was folded up and stored in a bay of the lander (the lunar module). Each of its four wheels had its own electric drive (a 0.25 horsepower motor), and it ran on two 36-volt silver-zinc batteries that could not be recharged. NASA gives its mass as 210 kg and its estimated top speed as about 8 mph (about 13 km/h). Total distance driven: Apollo 15 about 28 km (27.8 km), Apollo 16 26.7 km, Apollo 17 about 36 km (35.9 km, but see notes: other NASA pages disagree). Mission rules kept the crews within 6 miles (about 10 km) of the lander, the distance they could walk back in a pinch; the farthest the rover actually got from the lander was 5.0 km (Apollo 15), 4.5 km (Apollo 16) and 7.6 km (Apollo 17).

NASA pages DISAGREE on this number: NSSDCA 35.9 km; NASA History 2022 '22.2 miles' (about 35.7 km); NASA History 2021 'nearly 22.5 miles'; NASA's Apollo 17 Mission Details page 30.5 km; the APOD page 'about 18 miles'. Best choice: 'about 36 km (22 miles)' sourced to NSSDCA, or avoid an exact figure. (2) Apollo 15: '27.9 km' was not found on any page I could open; NSSDCA says 27.8 km and NASA's Apollo 15 Mission Details says 17.5 miles (about 28 km), so say 'about 28 km'. That same Apollo 15 page also has a record-list line 'maximum radial distance traveled on the lunar surface away from the spacecraft of about 17.5 miles'; it contradicts NSSDCA's 5.0 km maximum range, so do NOT use it for distance from the lander. (3) Walk-back rule: NASA SP-350 says mission rules kept crews within 6 miles (about 10 km) of the LM, 'the distance we could walk back in a pinch'. 'In a pinch' is NASA's wording; 'if the rover failed' is my paraphrase. The farthest actual range was 7.6 km (Apollo 17), under the limit. I could not open NASA's Apollo Lunar Surface Journal pages (they redirect to its landing page for my tool), so I could not see how the walk-back limit was calculated. (4) Top speed: 'about 13 km/h (8 mph)' is NASA's ESTIMATED top speed (APOD). NASA pages differ: SP-350 'top speed of 7 mph'; the ALSJ page quoting the Apollo 15 Pilot's Report says '13 kilometers (7 miles) per hour' (internally inconsistent, 13 km is about 8 miles); a 2026 NASA abstract says design 9-13 km/h and up to 14 km/h on Apollo 16; downhill the crews went faster (see V2). Safe wording: 'about 13 km/h on level ground'. (5) Mass: NASA's NSSDCA sentence says 'mass of 210 kg'; the words 'on Earth' are not in it (mass is the same on the Moon; the weight would be about one sixth there). (6) Wheels: NSSDCA says 'woven ... steel strands'; the words 'wire mesh' are NASA wording only on a NASA Glenn page (www3.nasa.gov/specials/wheels/), so 'wire mesh wheels' is OK to use with that source. claim: NASA's own history article says the Apollo 17 crew, Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, set a lunar speed record of 18 km/h while driving downhill, on their way back to the lander on the third moonwalk. NASA's book Apollo Expeditions to the Moon says that going down the Lee-Lincoln scarp (a feature at the Apollo 17 landing site, per NASA Science) the crew set 'an informal lunar speed record for four-wheeled vehicles of 11 mph' (18 km/h is about 11.2 mph). The Apollo 16 crew had already radioed 17 km/h as 'a new world's speed record'.

notes: Status 'corrected': the core is confirmed on a NASA page, but the wording must change. (1) Who: NASA History says 'they' (Cernan and Schmitt); it does not name Cernan alone as setting the record. Cernan is named as driver elsewhere in the same article, so 'Cernan and Schmitt' or 'the Apollo 17 crew' is the safe wording. (2) 'Unofficial': NASA History states the record without a qualifier; the word 'informal' is NASA's, from SP-350, and SP-350 does not name the astronaut or the mission in that sentence (it ties it to the Lee-Lincoln scarp, which NASA Science places at the Apollo 17 site). Do not state which moonwalk or place on the card. (5) Do not say 'the first' or 'the only' record: on a NASA ALSJ transcript page the Apollo 16 crew radioed a 'new world's speed record' of 17 km/h on their third moonwalk (the page's own surrounding text points to John Young as speaker, but I did not see a speaker label on that exact line). (6) Non-NASA pages (Guinness World Records, Wikipedia, a Fox News piece) name Cernan, 18 km/h = 11.2 mph and the word 'unofficial'; I saw them only as search results, did not open them and did not use them. NASA's Apollo Lunar Surface Journal pages that discuss the record could not be opened by my tool (they redirect to its landing page), so I could not check the original transcript. claim: NASA says its Lunar Terrain Vehicle (LTV) is a new rover for Artemis astronauts exploring the Moon's South Pole region, so they can go farther and do more science than before. It will work like a cross between an Apollo-style lunar rover (astronauts drive it) and a Mars-style uncrewed rover: between crew missions it can be operated remotely (NASA's October 2026 update says remotely operated from Earth) to carry cargo and science payloads to new landing sites and to map the surface before crews arrive. NASA plans to contract the LTV as a service from industry instead of owning it. Contract status: in April 2024 NASA selected Intuitive Machines, Lunar Outpost and Venturi Astrolab for year-long feasibility studies; on 26 May 2026 NASA awarded Astrolab ($219 million) and Lunar Outpost ($220 million) to build and deliver the first phase of LTVs, to reach the lunar surface by 2028; as of 20 Oct 2026 NASA says both companies are on schedule to deliver flight-ready hardware to NASA at the end of 2027.
